title: An ordinary day
goal: Talk about your daily routine, use verbs with *się*, and say how often you do things.
bekal: using *się* verbs and knowing where *się* can go
telling the story of a whole day in order

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jak wygląda twój dzień?
dialogs.intro: A long table in the campus canteen. The conversation turns to everyone's habits.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Budzę się o wpół do siódmej. Potem myję się i ubieram się.
lines.id: I wake up at half past six. Then I wash and get dressed.
lines.literal: I-wake self at half to seventh. then I-wash self and I-dress self.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Tak wcześnie? Ja wstaję o siódmej.
lines.id: That early? I get up at seven.
lines.literal: so early? I get-up at seventh.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Uczę się rano, bo wtedy najlepiej się koncentruję.
lines.id: I study in the morning, because that's when I focus best.
lines.literal: I-teach self morning, because then best self I-concentrate.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: A ja uczę się wieczorem. Rano tylko piję kawę i czytam wiadomości.
lines.id: I study in the evening. In the morning I just drink coffee and read the news.
lines.literal: and I teach self evening. morning only I-drink coffee and I-read news.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Trzy razy w tygodniu, po zajęciach. A ty?
lines.id: Three times a week, after class. And you?
lines.literal: three times in week, after classes. and you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rzadko. Czasem biegam w parku w niedzielę.
lines.id: Rarely. Sometimes I run in the park on Sundays.
lines.literal: rarely. sometimes I-run in park in Sunday.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: And what time do you go to bed?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zwykle o jedenastej. W weekend później.
lines.id: Usually at eleven. Later on weekends.
lines.literal: usually at eleventh. in weekend later.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Ja też. W sobotę nie budzę się przed dziesiątą.
lines.id: Me too. On Saturdays I don't get up before ten.
lines.literal: I too. in Saturday not I-wake self before tenth.

notes: **Się doesn't mean anything on its own.** It shows that the action comes back to the doer: *budzę* = I wake (someone else), *budzę się* = I wake up (myself). English often handles this with "myself" or just leaves it out; Polish uses one small word next to the verb.
**Się moves around**, and that's not a typo. *Uczę się rano* and *Rano się uczę* are both correct. There's only one rule: *się* **can never be the first word** in a sentence.
**Najlepiej się koncentruję** — here *się* comes before the verb. Poles tend to attach *się* to the stressed word, and your ear will catch this tendency long before your head can explain it.
**Myję się** literally means "I wash myself" and is the everyday way to say you wash or shower. For a bath you say *kąpię się*. Polish has no single all-purpose word for "bathing".
**Trzy razy w tygodniu** — "three times a week". *Raz* (once), *dwa razy* (twice), *pięć razy* (five times) — the 2-3-4 number rule you already know is at work again.

**Po zajęciach** — "after class". The preposition *po* takes the *miejscownik* you just learned, here in the plural: *zajęcia → zajęciach*. The *-ach* ending marks the plural *miejscownik* for every noun type without exception — one of the easiest endings in Polish.
**O której się kładziesz** — literally "at what time do you lay yourself down". For sleeping there are two different words: *kłaść się spać* (go to bed) and *spać* (be asleep).
**Brzmi rozsądnie** — "sounds sensible". Notice there's no "it": a Polish verb in the *on/ona/ono* form can stand alone without a subject when it's clear what's meant.

grammars.title: Verbs with się
body: The forms are perfectly regular — the only thing to manage is where *się* goes.
after: *Się* **never changes form**, whoever the subject is. One word, six persons — one of the easiest things in all of Polish.

Three placement rules are enough for A1: (1) never at the start of a sentence, (2) usually right after its verb, (3) in longer sentences it often jumps in front of the verb. All three are correct; none of them is wrong.

⚠️ Some verbs change meaning completely without *się*: *uczyć* (to teach) vs *uczyć się* (to learn), *budzić* (to wake someone) vs *budzić się* (to wake up). Never drop *się* just because the sentence feels complete.

grammars.title: How often
body: Two ways: a single adverb, or a count with *raz*.
after: Note that *nigdy* always pairs with *nie*: *Nigdy nie piję alkoholu*. Dropping *nie* doesn't make the sentence shorter, just broken — unlike English "never".
Frequency adverbs usually come **before** the verb: *Często czytam*, *Rzadko biegam*. Putting them at the start of the sentence is also correct, and very common.

blocks.text: Read these aloud twice, then cover the right-hand column and tell the story of your own day using these sentences.

head: Polski
English
rows: I wake up at half past six.
I get dressed and have breakfast.
I take the bus to the university.
During the break I have coffee with friends.
In the evening I study for two hours.
I go to bed at eleven.

blocks.title: Linking words that make a story flow
items: *zawsze najpierw…, a potem…* — always first…, and then…
These five words turn a list of short sentences into a story. Start using them now, even while your sentences are still simple.

blocks.text: Notice that *grać* takes two different prepositions: *grać **w*** for games (*w piłkę*, *w szachy*) and *grać **na*** for instruments (*na gitarze*, *na pianinie*). These are fixed pairs — learn them as a set.

blocks.title: Asking about other people's habits
items: *Co robisz w wolnym czasie?* — What do you do in your free time?
*O której wstajesz?* — What time do you get up?
*Masz jakieś hobby?* — Do you have any hobbies?
